data.text/markdown:
Packed-bed reactor: hot spots and runaway, step by step

Editable companion to the interactive page. Each step explains one piece of the 2D pseudo-homogeneous model and of its solution by the method of lines, runs it, and shows the result. The same code is shown, with the same explanations, in the page's Python (step by step) tab. To run: once the notebook has loaded, run all cells (command palette → "Re-run all cells", or the run button). To experiment: edit a value in the USER_INPUTS cell below and re-run; every cell that depends on it recomputes. The reference module pbr (finite-volume grid, rate law, right-hand side, Jacobian, Rosenbrock integrator, scipy BDF check, finite-difference sensitivities) is embedded in the next cell. A syntax-highlighted listing is in the page's pbr.py (full source) tab.

Step 1: Inputs and dimensionless groups

Everything starts from the dimensional inputs of Froment's o-xylene tube. A dictionary maps names to SI values. In the live run, USER_INPUTS holds the values from the sidebar; at build time it is empty. groups_from_dimensional condenses the 17 inputs into the 8 numbers the equations actually depend on (Theory §3). Two of them tell most of the story:
  • ||(S||) is the heat the feed can release, measured in units of ||(RT_0^2/E||) (about 29 K here).
  • ||(N = St/Da||) is the 1D cooling capacity relative to the reaction rate at the inlet.
Semenov's criterion (Theory §9) says to worry when ||(N/S||) approaches ||(e \approx 2.7||).

data.text/markdown:
Step 2: The radial grid: finite volumes

We cut the cross-section into ||(N||) rings ("cells") of equal width ||(d = 1/N||). Each cell stores one ||(x||) and one ||(\theta||) at its centre. The Laplacian becomes flux in minus flux out, divided by the ring's area ||(V_i||):
  • cw[i] and ce[i] are the weights of the inner and outer neighbours.
  • At the axis the inner face has radius 0, so cw[0] = 0 and no flux crosses it. That is the symmetry condition, with no special-casing.
  • ce[N-1] = 0 too, because the wall face is handled by the Robin condition (next cell).

Step 3: Checking the discrete Laplacian and the wall condition

Test: for ||(u = \rho^2||) the exact Laplacian is ||(\frac{1}{\rho}(\rho\cdot 2\rho)' = 4||) everywhere. Finite volumes reproduce this exactly in every interior cell, including the axis cell, because the flux ||(\rho\,u'||) is linear in ||(\rho^2||). At the wall the Robin condition ||(-\partial\theta/\partial\rho = Bi(\theta_R-\theta_w)||) is applied half a cell away from the last centre. Eliminating the unknown wall value gives ||(Bi_{\text{eff}} = Bi/(1 + Bi\,d/2)||) (Theory §5).

data.text/markdown:
Step 4: The rate law and the Arrhenius feedback

The dimensionless rate is ||(r = (1-x)\exp(\theta/(1+\theta/\gamma))||). Each unit of ||(\theta||) (about 29 K) multiplies the rate by roughly ||(e||). Unchecked, that positive feedback (hotter means faster, which means hotter still) is what turns a hot spot into runaway. With finite ||(\gamma||) the growth is slightly sub-exponential, which is why real runaway is a little milder than the ||(\gamma\to\infty||) textbook picture.

Step 5: The right-hand side: unknowns interleaved per cell

The state vector stores [x0, th0, x1, th1, ...]. Python slicing gives y[0::2] (all conversions) and y[1::2] (all temperatures), so rhs is written with whole-array numpy operations and no Python loop. At the inlet (||(x = 0||), ||(\theta = 0||)) the temperature is uniform, so dispersion contributes nothing. Every cell heats at the rate ||(S\,Da||), and every cell converts at the rate ||(Da||).

data.text/markdown:
Step 6: The Jacobian: five diagonals

Implicit methods need the Jacobian ||(J = \partial f/\partial y||). With interleaved unknowns it is banded:
  • reaction couples ||(x_i||) and ||(\theta_i||) (offsets ±1);
  • dispersion couples a cell to its neighbours (offsets ±2).
So only 5 diagonals are non-zero, whatever ||(N||) is. The figure shows the sparsity pattern. We check the hand-derived Jacobian against finite differences of rhs. A small mismatch would silently slow the solver down. Rust avoids the question entirely by computing the rate derivatives with automatic differentiation.

Step 7: Why the problem is stiff

The eigenvalues of ||(J||) set the time scales of the system. Their spread is the stiffness ratio. An explicit method such as forward Euler is only stable for ||(h < 2/|\lambda|_{max}||). That limit is set by the fastest radial mode, about ||(a_h N^2||), even though the solution changes slowly almost everywhere. Implicit and Rosenbrock methods have no such limit: their step is set by accuracy, not stability.

data.text/markdown:
Step 8: One Rosenbrock step, written out

This is the ode23s step (Theory §6), written out for a single step of size ||(h||). Each stage solves a linear system with the same matrix ||(W = I - h\,d\,J||). The matrix is linear, so there is no Newton iteration, and it is banded, so solve_banded is ||(O(N)||). The two solutions of different order differ by err. That difference estimates the local error and drives the step-size control. pbr.integrate runs exactly this loop with acceptance tests added.

console.text:
theta on the axis after one step: 0.011953515070925876
estimated local error (max)     : 1.04e-04

data.text/markdown:
Step 9: The full solve and the adaptive step size

Now we march the whole bed. The step size is the clearest picture of what the solver is doing:
  • it shrinks by orders of magnitude to resolve the hot spot, where temperature and reaction rate change fastest;
  • it relaxes again downstream, once the reactant is depleted.
A fixed step small enough for the hot spot would waste most of its effort elsewhere.

data.text/markdown:
Step 10: The temperature field

The 2D field shows what a 1D model cannot: the axis is far hotter than the wall region, because heat produced at the centre must be conducted across the bed before the coolant can remove it. The radial profile at the hot spot is close to a parabola, the shape behind the ||(R/(4\lambda_{er})||) term of the 1D–2D link.

data.text/markdown:
Step 11: Independent confirmation with scipy (BDF)

Agreement with our own Rosenbrock code only proves the code does what we wrote. For an independent check we hand the same rhs and Jacobian to scipy.integrate.solve_ivp with method="BDF". That is a variable-order multistep method with different error control. Agreement at tight tolerances confirms the time integration. The model and the spatial discretization are shared, and are checked separately (Bessel series and grid order in test_pbr.py).

data.text/markdown:
Step 12: 2D versus 1D

The 1D model sees one cross-sectional average temperature and lumps all resistance into ||(1/U = 1/\alpha_w + R/(4\lambda_{er})||). Its hot spot is milder than the axis temperature of the 2D model, and it also predicts runaway later. Designing with the 1D model alone is therefore non-conservative for wide tubes.

console.text:

data.text/markdown:
Step 13: Parametric sensitivity by finite differences, and its pitfall

The normalized sensitivity ||(s = (\phi/T^*)\,dT^*/d\phi||) by central differences needs two extra solves per parameter. Choosing the step ||(h||) is the catch:
  • a large ||(h||) sees the curvature of ||(T^*(\phi)||) (truncation error, which falls like ||(h^2||));
  • a small ||(h||) divides solver noise of relative size about rtol by ||(h||) (that error grows like ||(1/h||)).
The error curve is therefore V-shaped, and near runaway, where it matters most, the good window narrows. The Rust code avoids the choice entirely with automatic differentiation (Theory §8).

data.text/markdown:
Step 14: Morbidelli–Varma: sweep and find the critical feed

Sweep the feed partial pressure ||(p_0||), compute ||(T^*||) and ||(s||) at each value, and find the maximum of ||(|s|||). That maximum is the MV critical value ||(p_{0,c}||) (Theory §10). Below it the hot spot responds gently. Around it, a few percent more feed moves the hot spot by hundreds of kelvin. This sweep needs 3 solves per point, which takes seconds in Python. The App tab does the same with Rust in milliseconds.

Step 15: Semenov's limit for these inputs

Finally we place the current inputs on Semenov's map. With finite ||(\gamma||) the tangency condition ||(\theta_c = (1+\theta_c/\gamma)^2||) gives the critical ||(N/S||) (Theory §9). Semenov ignores consumption, so it is conservative: below the Semenov value runaway is possible, and the MV criterion tells how close you really are.
